title: Routine synaptic-resolution connectomics of entire mammalian brains

concept.text: The innovation would make it practical to reconstruct the synaptic wiring of an entire mammalian brain repeatedly. A connectome identifies individual neurons, follows their branching processes and assigns synaptic connections to the cells they join. Whole-brain coverage would allow researchers to trace connections across distant regions as well as within local circuits, without the boundaries imposed by small tissue fragments.

Whole-brain coverage and practical repetition jointly define this proposed advance. One exceptionally labor-intensive reconstruction would demonstrate an important part of the capability, but routine connectomics would also require reproducible accuracy and manageable demands on imaging, computation, elapsed time and human proofreading. An adult mouse brain is a concrete initial target; success in mice would not establish routine mapping across mammalian species.

Here, a complete connectome means an operationally comprehensive anatomical reconstruction with measured omissions and errors. It does not mean a flawless inventory of every synapse or a record of every physiological property. The adult fly precedent illustrates this distinction: its whole-brain chemical-synapse map remains valuable despite missing synapses, incomplete attachment of fine branches and exclusion of electrical synapses.

significance.text: The revolutionary capability would be a transition from mammalian cortical fragments to quantitative wiring maps that span an entire brain and can be compared across brains. Fragment boundaries interrupt pathways and leave their destinations outside the reconstruction. Whole-brain coverage can reveal connections that fragments cannot resolve; the fly work demonstrates this advantage by tracing pathways across the brain’s midline. Extending comparable coverage to mammals would expose local and long-range wiring within one integrated anatomical map.

If reliable whole-brain reconstruction became practical to repeat, researchers could compare wiring across individuals, ages, experiences, behavioral performance and disease states. Helmstaedter’s review motivates these applications through repeated mapping of comparatively smaller circuits; whole-mammalian-brain screening is the proposed extension. Repetition would enable researchers to estimate individual variation and test biological effects, but meaningful separation would still require adequate sample sizes, suitable controls and explicit estimates of reconstruction error.

An anatomical map would provide a powerful substrate for studying computation, but it would not by itself establish how a circuit produces its activity. The MICrONS authors explicitly distinguish wiring information from sufficient prediction of neuronal firing. Predicting computation from connectivity remains the separate challenge represented by NEU-03. Likewise, routine reconstruction of many whole human brains would require a further scaling advance beyond an initial rodent capability.

missing_breakthrough.text: The central unsolved capability is an audited, entire mammalian synaptic connectome that can be produced repeatedly with practical labor, time and resource requirements. The supplied 2024–2025 studies document roughly cubic-millimeter mammalian cortical reconstructions. Helmstaedter’s review, published in December 2025, identifies centimetre-scale circuits such as a whole adult mouse brain as a remaining challenge. Screening smaller circuits is already becoming possible; the missing advance concerns routine whole-brain mammalian reconstruction.

The engineering challenge spans the reconstruction pipeline: serial-section electron microscopy, alignment of images, segmentation of cells and their processes, identification of synapses, assignment of their cellular partners and correction of reconstruction errors. Scaling these stages must preserve enough continuity to follow long axons and fine branches across regions. Accurate synapse detection alone cannot establish accurate long-range connectivity if a process is interrupted or assigned to the wrong neuron. This is an engineering synthesis of the pipeline and audit distinctions described in the supplied review.

Human correction remains a major bottleneck. MICrONS identifies proofreading and analysis as its largest expense in person-hours, and extensive proofreading was concentrated on a subset of neurons. The breakthrough therefore requires reducing correction effort while maintaining demonstrable reconstruction quality across the whole brain. The supplied evidence establishes a labor problem but does not provide an accepted numerical threshold for affordable whole-brain screening.

current_state.text: In 2024, Dorkenwald and colleagues and the FlyWire Consortium reported a wiring diagram of an adult female Drosophila melanogaster brain containing 139,255 reconstructed neurons and approximately 50 million chemical synapses. This is a whole-brain achievement in a small nervous system. Its scope includes acknowledged missing synapses and incomplete attachment of fine branches, and excludes electrical synapses; describing it as complete should retain those qualifications.

In 2025, the MICrONS Consortium reported an electron-microscopy reconstruction of mouse visual cortex containing more than 200,000 cells and approximately 0.5 billion synapses. The reported in vivo dimensions were 1.3 × 0.87 × 0.82 mm, corresponding to roughly 0.93 mm³ and appropriately described as cubic-millimeter scale. This was a cortical fragment rather than a complete brain or complete cortical area. Proofreading covered a subset of neurons, so the dataset’s overall scale should not be confused with uniform manual verification of every reconstructed cell.

MICrONS also provides precedents for quantitative reconstruction audits. The supplied review reports synapse-detection precision and recall assessed against manual annotations, and an estimated partner-assignment accuracy of 98% from 191 manually annotated synapses held out from training. These measurements concern particular audited tasks and samples; they do not establish 98% accuracy for every aspect of the reconstruction or for long-range tracing across an entire brain. The associated reporting summary states that no experimental replication was performed.

In 2024, Shapson-Coe and colleagues reported a reconstruction of approximately one cubic millimeter of human temporal cortex, with about 57,000 cells, 230 millimeters of blood vessels and 150 million synapses. The tissue was removed during surgery to gain access to an underlying epileptic focus. This establishes a substantial human cortical-fragment reconstruction, not whole-human-brain coverage; its surgical provenance also matters when interpreting its biological representativeness.

Helmstaedter’s review was published on 8 December 2025 and appears in Nature Reviews Neuroscience volume 27, pages 101–120 (2026). Its available abstract describes accessible synaptic-resolution volumes as reaching approximately 1 mm³ and identifies whole-brain synaptic connectomes of small reptiles, rodents, birds and non-human primates as the next major target. It specifically identifies whole adult mouse brains as challenging. These are dated assessments and future targets, not demonstrations that the proposed whole-brain mammalian capability has been achieved.

The review’s extracted historical volume comparison remains unresolved. The supplied text combines an approximately 1,000-fold expansion with endpoints rendered as about 100 µm³ and 1 mm³. Taken literally, those endpoints imply a ten-million-fold volume increase, so the baseline notation and growth factor cannot both be reused as verified quantities. The approximately 1 mm³ endpoint is separately supported by the mammalian reconstructions; the earlier endpoint requires checking against the typeset original.

These conclusions rely on the supplied research and evidence review, whose access was uneven. The fly article was represented by a truncated alternative XML extraction. MICrONS HTML and article-PDF extractions were truncated, and the PDF extraction warned that some form content was skipped; its associated reporting summary and peer-review file were supplied in full. The human study was available through an abstract and extended-summary page, while Helmstaedter’s review was assessed through a subscription preview and abstract. These limitations constrain interpretation without negating the passages retained in the review. No bounded freshness search was supplied, so the documented milestones do not establish the largest mammalian reconstruction or the field’s latest status as of 1 November 2026.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: reconstruct one entire adult mouse brain at synaptic resolution, with independently audited coverage and accuracy sufficient to quantify both local and long-range cell-to-cell connectivity. Report the reconstruction’s anatomical scope, omissions and error estimates so that whole-brain coverage is assessable. This is a proposed convincing demonstration, not a published consensus standard.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility demonstration: reconstruct a second entire adult mouse brain at comparable quality with substantially less human proofreading. Report human hours, elapsed time, imaging resources and computational resources for both brains, allowing the claimed improvement to be evaluated against its resource costs. A second equivalent volume could be a useful intermediate scaling demonstration, but it would not by itself establish repeatability across whole brains because it could omit whole-brain integration challenges.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed reproducibility demonstration

completion_criteria.text: Proposed audit design: measure synapse-detection precision and recall, cellular partner-assignment accuracy and neurite continuity against held-out manual annotations sampled across brain regions and process types. Independent auditing should address both local synaptic errors and tracing errors that alter distant connectivity. MICrONS supplies a precedent for manual-label and held-out partner-assignment checks; extending these checks to distributed whole-brain coverage and long-range continuity is part of the proposal.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed audit design

completion_criteria.text: Proposed practical boundary: define acceptable quality and resource requirements for the intended comparative study before claiming routine use. No numerical cost cutoff or universal error threshold is established here. Two successful mouse reconstructions would demonstrate an initial whole-brain capability and repetition under those conditions; broader claims would require additional brains, biological variation and species-specific validation. Finite demonstrations establish tested breadth, not literal universality across mammalian brains.
completion_criteria.label: Proposed practical boundary

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis — NEU-01, “Simultaneous spike-resolved recording from every neuron in one behaving mammalian brain,” concerns whole-brain activity over time. NEU-02 concerns synaptic anatomy. The two would provide complementary observations, but a wiring reconstruction does not itself record spikes during behavior.

NEU-03, “A prospective theory that predicts mammalian circuit computation from connectivity,” is the closest conceptual neighbor. NEU-02 would provide anatomical inputs for such a theory, while NEU-03 would have to establish predictive relationships between connectivity and computation. The MICrONS authors’ clarification that wiring alone is not sufficient to predict firing supports this distinction. The supplied roster provides NEU-03’s title, not a fuller specification.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-04, “Content-faithful reading and writing of specific episodic memories,” would require identifying and manipulating particular remembered content. Connectomic comparisons might help investigate anatomical correlates, but a synaptic map does not itself decode a memory or demonstrate the ability to write one.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-05, “Target-specific regrowth of long axons in the adult mammalian central nervous system,” concerns repairing projections. NEU-06, “Reconstruction of human cognitive circuits after neurons have been lost,” concerns restoring circuits after cell loss. Whole-brain connectomics could provide anatomical reference maps and help assess reconstructed connections, while regrowth, neuronal replacement and functional restoration remain separate capabilities.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-07, “Noninvasive cellular-resolution read and write through the intact adult human skull,” concerns access to living human brain cells without invasive exposure. NEU-09, “Cell-type-specific molecular access throughout the intact adult human brain,” concerns selective molecular targeting. Both differ from the tissue-based electron-microscopy reconstruction underlying NEU-02: anatomical mapping would not establish either noninvasive read/write access or molecular delivery.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-08, “A generative developmental code that builds a specified functional neural circuit,” concerns constructing a desired circuit. NEU-02 concerns measuring existing wiring and could help compare intended with resulting anatomy. Structural agreement alone would not demonstrate that the constructed circuit performs the specified function.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-10, “A causal, measurement-grade account of conscious content,” requires an explanatory and causal account beyond anatomical description. NEU-11, “Reversible, circuit-specific reopening of critical-period plasticity in the adult brain,” concerns controlling plasticity. Connectomics could contribute anatomical constraints or comparisons to either effort, but neither causal explanation nor reversible control follows from a wiring map.

Roster-based synthesis — NEU-12, “A sufficient account of sleep that lets its necessary brain functions be completed without a normal sleep period,” concerns identifying and replacing sleep’s necessary functions. Comparing connectomes might contribute evidence about structural changes associated with sleep, but anatomical reconstruction alone would not establish those functions or a substitute for sleep.

change_log.change: Defined the advance through both whole-brain coverage and practical repetition, with an adult mouse as an initial demonstration.
change_log.reason: A single labor-intensive reconstruction would establish only part of the concept, and mouse success would not establish applicability across mammals.

change_log.change: Replaced the unqualified mammalian-record assertion with dated 2024–2025 milestones and an explicit freshness limitation.
change_log.reason: The supplied evidence documents those achievements but contains no bounded search establishing the latest record as of 1 November 2026.

change_log.change: Qualified the fly connectome’s completeness while retaining its whole-brain achievement and quantitative scale.
change_log.reason: The supplied review identifies missing synapses, incomplete fine-branch attachment and exclusion of electrical synapses.

change_log.change: Integrated mouse dimensions, cell and synapse counts, selective proofreading, audit measurements and lack of experimental replication; retained the human fragment’s quantitative detail and surgical provenance.
change_log.reason: These details distinguish reconstruction scale, verification scope and biological sampling without treating them as equivalent measures of completeness.

change_log.change: Separated smaller-circuit screening from the proposed extension to whole mammalian brains and added sampling, control and measurement-error requirements.
change_log.reason: The review supports comparative applications, but repeated mapping alone does not guarantee separation of biological effects from individual variation.

change_log.change: Preserved the unresolved historical volume comparison instead of presenting its extracted baseline or growth factor as settled.
change_log.reason: The stated endpoints imply a ten-million-fold increase, conflicting with the extracted 1,000-fold claim; the supplied material does not resolve the notation.

change_log.change: Strengthened the proposed demonstration to require a second whole brain at comparable quality and measured effort, with equivalent volume retained as an intermediate milestone.
change_log.reason: Equivalent volume can omit integration challenges specific to entire brains, and reduced proofreading is interpretable only alongside quality and resource measurements.

change_log.change: Expanded proposed audits beyond synapse detection to partner assignment and neurite continuity.
change_log.reason: Local detection accuracy does not establish correct long-range cell-to-cell connectivity.

change_log.change: Preserved access and extraction limitations and explained relationships to every other supplied roster entry.
change_log.reason: The final record must distinguish the evidence actually available from broader inferences and keep neighboring innovations separate.

unresolved_issues: The supplied evidence does not establish the field’s latest achievements or largest mammalian reconstruction as of 1 November 2026; no new research was performed.
The typeset historical starting-volume notation and its relationship to the claimed 1,000-fold expansion remain unresolved.
No numerical resource threshold, acceptable whole-brain error budget or agreed definition of routine screening is supplied. These would need to be specified for a concrete demonstration.
The evidence does not establish whether proofreading reductions can be maintained at comparable quality across complete brains, regions, process types or mammalian species.
Only titles are supplied for neighboring roster concepts, so their relationships are conceptual comparisons rather than assessments of their detailed requirements or evidence.
